title: Snowplow latency-cost vignette
content:
Purpose:
A compact bench vignette exploring a heuristic we nicknamed 'snowplow' — a light-touch approach to handling microbursty session traffic that mixes opportunistic prefetching with tightened admission for tail protection. The goal: illustrate latency vs $/query tradeoffs across three operating points and provide pragmatic knobs for product to ship as a guidance snippet in the Optimize docs.

High-level finding (TL;DR):
- Snowplow reduces p99 bursts by ~25–40% relative to naive small-batch routing while increasing $/Q by 6–12% depending on burst mix.
- Best fit for sessionized workloads with short prompts and occasional 2–10x momentary QPS spikes (mobile chat, query assistants).
- Recommended quick defaults: prefetch depth = 2 requests, admission headroom = 10%, fall back to async decode at sustained > 1.8x baseline.

Test setup (sanity checklist):
- Hardware: 2x A100 80GB per worker node, 8 workers per cluster, nvlink configured; baseline cluster used single-region core (us-west-2).
- Model: Llama2-13B-ptq (q4) — representative medium-context open model used in internal tests.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v0.9.2 with continuous batching enabled.
- Load profile: baseline steady QPS = 100 req/s; microburst profile injects 1-minute bursts to 300 req/s at Poisson arrival windows (bursts every 12 minutes).
- Request mix: 70% short (avg 32 tokens), 20% medium (avg 128 tokens), 10% long (avg 512 tokens).
- Metric collection: per-request p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput, and amortized $/query derived from internal cost model (GPU-minute + infra overhead).
- Caveats: single model family/hardware; results sensitive to model size and quantization profile. Consider this a heuristic demonstration rather than a canonical benchmark.

Operating points tested:
1) Naive small-batch (baseline): small-batch_max = 8, no prefetch, aggressive preempt disabled.
2) Big-tiling opportunistic: batch_max = 64, predictive prefetch=on (depth 4), tiling enabled (higher amortization).
3) Snowplow hybrid (our vignette): batch_max = 32, predictive prefetch depth = 2, admission headroom = 10%, async decode fallback when sustained > 1.8x baseline.

ASCII cost/latency table (aggregated across runs):

Mode           | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | queries/min | $/Q (normalized)
---------------|---------|---------|---------|-------------|-------------------
Naive small    |   120   |   280   |   920   |    6000     |       1.00        
Big-tiling     |   140   |   330   |   760   |    6300     |       0.88        
Snowplow       |   130   |   295   |   580   |    6200     |       1.06        

Interpretation: Snowplow sits between naive small-batch and big-tiling on latency while slightly increasing cost relative to baseline. Big-tiling reduces $/Q via higher packing but leaves a heavier tail (p99) due to bigger multiplex windows and slower cold-path reaction. Snowplow sacrifices a small amount of amortization to protect tails.

Burst fidelity breakdown (p99 during injected bursts):
- Naive small-batch: median p99_delta ≈ +420ms (from steady p99). Observed large spike variability across tenants.
- Big-tiling: median p99_delta ≈ +280ms, but heavy right tail (occasional >1.2s) due to batch formation delays and queueing.
- Snowplow: median p99_delta ≈ +160ms, few outliers >700ms.

Why the improvements? (short, actionable reasoning)
- Prefetch depth = 2 gives early KV warmup for session state and prefixes, reducing token generation setup. It avoids the over-aggressive prefetch depth of big-tiling which increases mis-prefetch waste.
- Admission headroom (10%) ensures a small spare share of slots to absorb arrival variance; this reduces queue tailing without large capacity overprovision.
- Async decode fallback reduces head-blocking on heavy requests at sustained overloads, pushing work to a cheaper path while preserving low-latency completion for most requests.

Parameter sensitivity (quick notes):
- Prefetch depth = 1: under-provisions; p99 rises ~10–15% vs depth=2.
- Prefetch depth = 4: improves steady $/Q but increases false warmups (waste) by ~18% and slightly worsens p90 in microbursts.
- Admission headroom 5%: insufficient for 2–3x spikes; 20%: reduces p99 further but increases $/Q by ~18% — marginal returns beyond 10%.

Visual-style sketch (text): session mix vs operating point (tokenized buckets)
- Short sessions dominate (70%) => most wins come from light prefetch + admission headroom.
- Workloads with >30% long requests prefer tiling (big-tiling) because amortization matters more than tail smoothing.

Practical defaults for product/docs (starter recipe):
- Default Snowplow profile (recommended for sessionized chat): prefetch_depth=2, admission_headroom=10%, batch_max=32, async_decode_threshold=1.8x, sampling: enable p99 sampling per tenant.
- Developer note: place a user-config toggle in console: "burst-smoothing: snowplow (default for chat)" with brief tooltip explaining tail vs cost tradeoff.

Operational guidance and checks:
- Monitoring: surface p99 delta during bursts in Console; if p99_delta > 300ms for >5min, auto-suggest switching to higher admission headroom or enable canary tiling.
- Billing: flag increased $/Q for Snowplow in receipts as a labeled line item ("burst smoothing"), roughly +8% estimate for typical chat mixes.
- Rollout: start as opt-in on Dedicated clusters, pilot with 3 midsize customers for 2 weeks before promoting to Hosted defaults.

Open questions & next experiments:
- Run the same mosaic with a larger model (70B q4) and with memory-constrained nodes (A100 40GB) to quantify model-size sensitivity.
- Evaluate Snowplow combined with KV cache sharing across co-located sessions (might reduce $/Q further).
- Microbenchmark: tighten async decode threshold sweep (1.4x–2.2x) to map knee-point for different session mixes.

Appendix: short runbook for reproducing the vignette
1) Checkout perf harness: github:repo/perf-harness commit sha: a3b9f2c
2) Start cluster-variant: ./scripts/deploy_cluster --nodes 8 --gpu a100-80gb --runtime v0.9.2
3) Load profile: ./tools/loadgen --profile snowplow-mix --baseline 100 --burst 300 --burst-interval 720s --duration 2h
4) Collect traces: prometheus push + payload logs to s3://redwood-perf/snowplow/2026-03-12/*
